title: Paella Valenciana
subtitle: Saffron rice with chicken, chorizo and prawns
excerpt: Chicken legs, chorizo and king prawns cooked in a wide pan with saffron-scented rice and smoky tomato broth. The socarrat, the toasted, slightly crispy rice crust at the bottom of the pan, is what separates a good paella from a great one. This version uses short-grain rice and a wide frying pan as a practical substitute for a proper paella dish.
sourceNotes: Paella originates in the Valencia region of Spain and was traditionally cooked outdoors over an orange-wood fire; the dish was originally made with rabbit and snails before seafood and chicken versions spread worldwide.

content.text: The cardinal rule of paella is: never stir the rice once the stock has been added. Stirring releases starch, turns the texture gluey and prevents the socarrat from forming. Add the stock, distribute the ingredients evenly, then leave it alone. You'll know the socarrat is forming when you hear a light crackling sound from the bottom of the pan in the last few minutes of cooking.

items.prepNote: jointed into thigh and drumstick if large
half a tin, drained and roughly chopped

content.text: Heat the olive oil in a very wide frying pan (30cm or wider) over a high heat. Season the chicken pieces and brown on all sides for 8 to 10 minutes. Remove to a plate. Add the chorizo rounds and fry for 2 minutes until the oil is red. Remove.

Reduce the heat to medium. Cook the onion and red pepper in the same pan for 5 minutes until softened. Add the garlic and smoked paprika and cook for 1 minute. Add the tinned tomatoes and cook for 3 minutes, stirring, until the mixture darkens and thickens.

Tip in the rice and stir to coat every grain in the tomato mixture. Pour in the warm stock and the saffron water. Stir once to distribute everything evenly, then nestle the chicken pieces back in. Do not stir again.

Cook over a medium heat for 18 to 20 minutes until the stock is absorbed and the rice is just tender. In the last 5 minutes, lay the prawns on top and the chorizo rounds over the surface. They will cook from the steam.

In the final 2 minutes, increase the heat to high and listen for a light crackling from the bottom of the pan. This is the socarrat forming. Remove from the heat, cover with a clean cloth for 5 minutes, and serve straight from the pan.

items.symptom: Rice is still wet after 20 minutes
items.cause: Too much stock was added or the heat was too low to evaporate it properly
items.fix: Increase the heat to medium-high and cook uncovered for a further 3 to 5 minutes until the liquid is absorbed.

items.symptom: Bottom layer has burned rather than formed a crust
items.cause: Heat was too high in the final stage or the rice was cooked too long before the socarrat step
items.fix: Keep a close eye and ear on the pan in the final 2 minutes. A good socarrat smells toasted; burned rice smells acrid. Remove from the heat immediately if you smell burning.
